records.source: וַֽיִּשְׁמְע֔וּ צָרֵ֥י יְהוּדָ֖ה וּבִנְיָמִ֑ן כִּֽי־בְנֵ֤י הַגּוֹלָה֙ בּוֹנִ֣ים הֵיכָ֔ל לַיהוָ֖ה אֱלֹהֵ֥י יִשְׂרָאֵֽל׃
records.gloss: And heard [the] adversaries of Judah and Benjamin that [the] sons of the exile [were] building a temple for YHWH [the] God of Israel.
pieces: The enemies of Judah and Benjamin heard that the returned exiles were building a temple for {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} the God of Israel.

L.1: And the adversaries of Judah and Benjamin heard that the sons of the exile were building a temple for {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} the God of Israel.

R.1: The enemies of Judah and Benjamin heard that the people who came back from exile were building a temple for {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, the God of Israel.

decisions.choice: the adversaries of Judah and Benjamin: those who opposed the returned community
decisions.reason: The writer calls them adversaries from the start, before they say a word. They are the people of verse 2, settled in the land by the kings of Assyria, and later the officials of Samaria (verses 9-10, 17). Judah and Benjamin are the two tribes whose land the exiles came back to (1:5).

decisions.choice: the sons of the exile: the community of those who returned from Babylon
decisions.reason: "Sons of" here means members of a group. In Ezra the phrase names the returned exiles as a community (6:19-20; 8:35; 10:7, 16).

decisions.choice: the returned exiles (Balanced); the people who came back from exile (Readable)
decisions.reason: The Ezra term list gives these wordings; Literal keeps "the sons of the exile".

records.heading: The adversaries of Judah and Benjamin

records.source: וַיִּגְּשׁ֨וּ אֶל־זְרֻבָּבֶ֜ל וְאֶל־רָאשֵׁ֣י הָֽאָב֗וֹת וַיֹּאמְר֤וּ לָהֶם֙ נִבְנֶ֣ה עִמָּכֶ֔ם כִּ֣י כָכֶ֔ם נִדְר֖וֹשׁ לֵֽאלֹהֵיכֶ֑ם וְל֣וֹ׀אֲנַ֣חְנוּ זֹבְחִ֗ים מִימֵי֙ אֵסַ֤ר חַדֹּן֙ מֶ֣לֶךְ אַשּׁ֔וּר הַמַּעֲלֶ֥ה אֹתָ֖נוּ פֹּֽה׃
records.gloss: And they approached Zerubbabel and [the] heads of the fathers and said to them, let us build with you, for like you we seek your God, and to him we [have been] sacrificing since [the] days of Esarhaddon king of Assyria, who brought us up here.
pieces: So they came to Zerubbabel and the heads of families and said to them, "Let us build with you, for we worship your God as you do, and we have been sacrificing to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} ever since the days of Esarhaddon king of Assyria, who brought us here."

L.2: And they approached Zerubbabel and the heads of the fathers' [houses] and said to them, "Let us build with you, for like you we seek your God, and we have been sacrificing to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} since the days of Esarhaddon king of Assyria, who brought us up here."

R.2: So they came to Zerubbabel and the family leaders and said, "Let us help you build, because we worship your God just as you do. We have been offering sacrifices to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} ever since King Esarhaddon of Assyria brought us here."

decisions.choice: Esarhaddon king of Assyria: the king who settled them here
decisions.reason: Esarhaddon ruled Assyria from 681 to 669 BC. After the northern kingdom fell in 722 BC the kings of Assyria moved peoples from other lands into the cities of Samaria. They learned to worship the LORD but went on serving their own gods as well (2 Kings 17:24-41).

decisions.choice: to him we sacrifice: the reading of the Hebrew margin
alternatives: and we have not sacrificed since the days of Esarhaddon
decisions.reason: The written text has a word meaning "not", which would give "and we have not been sacrificing" since Esarhaddon's days. The scribes' marginal reading, followed here, has a word that sounds the same and means "to him". The marginal reading fits the claim the speakers are making.

decisions.choice: we seek your God: we worship him
decisions.reason: To "seek" God is to turn to him in worship and prayer (Deuteronomy 4:29; Psalm 105:4). They claim to share the returned exiles' faith; 2 Kings 17:33 says such settlers feared the LORD and served their own gods too.

decisions.choice: the heads of the fathers: heads of families
decisions.reason: As in 3:12, "the fathers" stands for the fathers' houses, the extended families.

decisions.choice: {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}
decisions.reason: The pronoun refers to God, so it takes the deity pronoun setting.

records.source: וַיֹּאמֶר֩ לָהֶ֨ם זְרֻבָּבֶ֜ל וְיֵשׁ֗וּעַ וּשְׁאָ֨ר רָאשֵׁ֤י הָֽאָבוֹת֙ לְיִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל לֹֽא־לָ֣כֶם וָלָ֔נוּ לִבְנ֥וֹת בַּ֖יִת לֵאלֹהֵ֑ינוּ כִּי֩ אֲנַ֨חְנוּ יַ֜חַד נִבְנֶ֗ה לַֽיהוָה֙ אֱלֹהֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל כַּאֲשֶׁ֣ר צִוָּ֔נוּ הַמֶּ֖לֶךְ כּ֥וֹרֶשׁ מֶֽלֶךְ־פָּרָֽס׃
records.gloss: And said to them Zerubbabel and Jeshua and [the] rest of [the] heads of the fathers of Israel, not for you and for us to build a house for our God, for we together will build for YHWH [the] God of Israel, as commanded us the king Cyrus, king of Persia.
pieces: But Zerubbabel, Jeshua and the rest of the heads of the families of Israel said to them, "You have no part with us in building a house for our God. We alone will build it for {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} the God of Israel, as King Cyrus, the king of Persia, commanded us."

L.3: And Zerubbabel and Jeshua and the rest of the heads of the fathers' [houses] of Israel said to them, "[It is] not for you and for us to build a house for our God, but we ourselves together will build for {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} the God of Israel, as King Cyrus the king of Persia commanded us."

R.3: But Zerubbabel, Jeshua and the other leaders of the families of Israel answered, "You have no part in building a temple for our God. We will build it ourselves for {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, the God of Israel, as King Cyrus of Persia commanded us."

decisions.choice: not for you and for us: you have no share with us
decisions.reason: "Not for you and for us" is a way of saying the two groups have nothing in common in this work (compare 2 Kings 9:18, "what is it to you", and Nehemiah 2:20, "you have no share").

decisions.choice: we together will build: we by ourselves
decisions.reason: The word means "together" or "as one"; set against "you" it means the returned exiles alone, as one body.

decisions.choice: as Cyrus commanded us: the decree was for his people
decisions.reason: Cyrus's decree invited those "among you of all his people" to go up and build (1:3), and it was the returned exiles who went. The leaders answer by appealing to the king's own terms. Verse 1 has already called those who asked adversaries, and verses 4-5 show what they did next.

decisions.choice: You have no part with us in (Balanced); You have no part in (Readable)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable give the sense of the short Hebrew phrase; Literal keeps its form with a bracketed verb.

records.source: וַיְהִי֙ עַם־הָאָ֔רֶץ מְרַפִּ֖ים יְדֵ֣י עַם־יְהוּדָ֑ה וּֽמְבַהֲלִ֥ים אוֹתָ֖ם לִבְנֽוֹת׃
records.gloss: And it was [that the] people of the land [were] weakening [the] hands of [the] people of Judah and terrifying them from building,
pieces: Then the people of the land set about discouraging the people of Judah and making them afraid to build,

L.4: And it was that the people of the land were weakening the hands of the people of Judah and making them afraid to build,

R.4: So the people living in the land tried to discourage the people of Judah and frighten them so they would stop building.

decisions.choice: the people of the land: the populations outside the returned community
decisions.reason: As in 3:3, the phrase means those who were not among the returned exiles, here the same people who asked to build in verse 2. Elsewhere it can mean the ordinary landholders of Judah (2 Kings 11:14), but in Ezra and Nehemiah it marks those outside the community of the return (9:1; 10:2).

decisions.choice: weakening the hands: discouraging them
decisions.reason: Hands that hang down picture people who have lost heart (Jeremiah 38:4; Nehemiah 6:9). The participles describe something they kept doing.

decisions.choice: terrifying them from building: making them afraid to build
decisions.reason: The Hebrew margin and the written text differ slightly in the form of this verb, but both mean to frighten or alarm.

decisions.choice: the people living in the land
decisions.reason: Readable follows the Ezra term list, as in 3:3.

decisions.choice: ending with a comma
decisions.reason: The sentence runs on into verse 5, so Literal and Balanced end the record with a comma; Readable ends its own sentence here.

records.source: וְסֹכְרִ֧ים עֲלֵיהֶ֛ם יוֹעֲצִ֖ים לְהָפֵ֣ר עֲצָתָ֑ם כָּל־יְמֵ֗י כּ֚וֹרֶשׁ מֶ֣לֶךְ פָּרַ֔ס וְעַד־מַלְכ֖וּת דָּרְיָ֥וֶשׁ מֶֽלֶךְ־פָּרָֽס׃
records.gloss: and hiring against them counselors to frustrate their purpose all [the] days of Cyrus king of Persia and until [the] reign of Darius king of Persia.
pieces: and they bribed officials against them to frustrate their plans throughout the reign of Cyrus king of Persia and until the reign of Darius king of Persia.

L.5: and hiring counselors against them to frustrate their purpose all the days of Cyrus king of Persia and until the reign of Darius king of Persia.

R.5: They paid officials to work against them and spoil their plans. This went on as long as Cyrus was king of Persia and until Darius became king.

decisions.choice: hiring counselors: paying advisers or officials to act against them
decisions.reason: The counselors are most likely people with influence at the Persian court or in the provincial government, paid to block the work. "Hire" is used of bribing a prophet in Nehemiah 6:12-13.

decisions.choice: from Cyrus to Darius: about eighteen years
decisions.reason: Cyrus ruled the Persian empire from 539 to 530 BC and Darius I from 522 to 486 BC. Work on the temple stopped until the second year of Darius, 520 BC (verse 24; Haggai 1:1-2).

decisions.choice: until the reign of Darius: the account moves ahead
decisions.reason: This verse sums up the whole time of opposition to the temple. Verses 6-23 then go further ahead to later kings, Ahasuerus and Artaxerxes, and to opposition against the city walls; verse 24 comes back to the temple under Darius.

decisions.choice: bribed officials
decisions.reason: Balanced says what "hiring counselors against them" amounted to; Literal keeps the words. Readable says "paid officials".

records.source: וּבְמַלְכוּת֙ אֲחַשְׁוֵר֔וֹשׁ בִּתְחִלַּ֖ת מַלְכוּת֑וֹ כָּתְב֣וּ שִׂטְנָ֔ה עַל־יֹשְׁבֵ֥י יְהוּדָ֖ה וִירוּשָׁלִָֽם׃ס
records.gloss: And in [the] reign of Ahasuerus, in [the] beginning of his reign, they wrote an accusation against [the] inhabitants of Judah and Jerusalem.
pieces: In the reign of Ahasuerus, at the beginning of his reign, they wrote an accusation against the people living in Judah and Jerusalem.

L.6: And in the reign of Ahasuerus, in the beginning of his reign, they wrote an accusation against the inhabitants of Judah and Jerusalem.

R.6: Later, when Ahasuerus became king, they wrote a letter accusing the people of Judah and Jerusalem.

decisions.choice: Ahasuerus: the Persian king known in Greek as Xerxes
decisions.reason: Ahasuerus is the king of the book of Esther, known in Greek as Xerxes I, who ruled the Persian empire from 486 to 465 BC, after Darius I. The beginning of his reign was some thirty years after the temple was finished (6:15).

decisions.choice: an accusation: a formal complaint
decisions.reason: The noun comes from the same root as the word for an adversary or accuser (compare Satan). Nothing more is said about this letter or its result.

decisions.choice: Later
decisions.reason: Readable adds "Later" to show that the account has moved on beyond Darius (meaning decision m3 at verse 5).

records.source: וּבִימֵ֣י אַרְתַּחְשַׁ֗שְׂתָּא כָּתַ֨ב בִּשְׁלָ֜ם מִתְרְדָ֤ת טָֽבְאֵל֙ וּשְׁאָ֣ר כְּנָוֺתָ֔יו עַל־אַרְתַּחְשַׁ֖שְׂתְּ מֶ֣לֶךְ פָּרָ֑ס וּכְתָב֙הַֽנִּשְׁתְּוָ֔ן כָּת֥וּב אֲרָמִ֖ית וּמְתֻרְגָּ֥ם אֲרָמִֽית׃פ
records.gloss: And in [the] days of Artaxerxes wrote Bishlam, Mithredath, Tabeel and [the] rest of his associates to Artaxerxes king of Persia; and [the] writing of the letter [was] written [in] Aramaic and translated [in] Aramaic.
pieces: And in the days of Artaxerxes, Bishlam, Mithredath, Tabeel and the rest of their associates wrote to Artaxerxes king of Persia. The letter was written in Aramaic script and translated into Aramaic.

L.7: And in the days of Artaxerxes, Bishlam, Mithredath, Tabeel and the rest of his associates wrote to Artaxerxes king of Persia; and the text of the letter was written in Aramaic [script] and translated [into] Aramaic.

R.7: Then, when Artaxerxes was king of Persia, Bishlam, Mithredath, Tabeel and the others with them wrote to him. The letter was written in Aramaic letters and in the Aramaic language.

decisions.choice: Artaxerxes: Artaxerxes I, king of Persia
decisions.reason: This is most likely Artaxerxes I, who ruled from 465 to 424 BC, after Ahasuerus. Ezra (7:1) and Nehemiah (Nehemiah 2:1) came to Jerusalem in his reign. So verses 7-23 concern events some seventy or more years after the temple's foundation, and they are about the city and its walls (verses 12-13), not the temple.

decisions.choice: Bishlam: probably a personal name
decisions.reason: The word is taken here as the name of one of the writers, like Mithredath and Tabeel. It could also be read as "with the agreement of", that is, Mithredath wrote with Tabeel's approval.

decisions.choice: written in Aramaic script and translated into Aramaic
alternatives: was written in Aramaic and translated. [The following is in] Aramaic:
decisions.reason: The first "Aramaic" can be read as the script and the second as the language: the letter was written in Aramaic letters and set out in the Aramaic language, the official language of the Persian empire. Another reading takes the last word as a note to the reader, "Aramaic:", marking that the text from here (4:8-6:18) is itself in Aramaic; the verse would then end "written in Aramaic and translated".

decisions.choice: their associates
decisions.reason: The Hebrew has "his associates", referring to the first named writer; Balanced and Readable say "their" ("with them") since three writers are named. Literal keeps "his".

decisions.choice: Aramaic [script] ... [into] Aramaic (Literal); Aramaic script ... into Aramaic (Balanced)
decisions.reason: English needs words to show the two senses of "Aramaic" that meaning decision m3 takes; Literal brackets them.

records.source: רְח֣וּם בְּעֵל־טְעֵ֗ם וְשִׁמְשַׁי֙ סָֽפְרָ֔א כְּתַ֛בוּ אִגְּרָ֥ה חֲדָ֖ה עַל־יְרוּשְׁלֶ֑ם לְאַרְתַּחְשַׁ֥שְׂתְּא מַלְכָּ֖א כְּנֵֽמָא׃
records.gloss: Rehum, master of decree, and Shimshai the scribe wrote a letter, one, concerning Jerusalem to Artaxerxes the king, as follows:
pieces: Rehum the chief officer and Shimshai the scribe wrote a letter against Jerusalem to King Artaxerxes, as follows:

L.8: Rehum the commander and Shimshai the scribe wrote a letter concerning Jerusalem to Artaxerxes the king, as follows:

R.8: Rehum the chief officer and Shimshai the secretary wrote a letter to King Artaxerxes against Jerusalem. This is what it said:

decisions.choice: the text changes from Hebrew to Aramaic
decisions.reason: From this verse to 6:18 the book is written in Aramaic, the language of the Persian empire's letters and records, which the Jews of the exile also spoke. The section quotes or follows official documents, beginning with this letter. The text returns to Hebrew at 6:19, and there is a second Aramaic section, the king's letter to Ezra, at 7:12-26.

decisions.choice: master of decree and the scribe: the senior official and the secretary
decisions.reason: "Master of decree" is a Persian title for a high official with authority to issue orders, perhaps the head of the provincial administration in Samaria. The scribe was the official secretary who wrote and kept the documents. Both seem to belong to the government of the province Beyond the River (verses 10, 17).

decisions.choice: a letter concerning Jerusalem: a letter against it
decisions.reason: The preposition means "about" or "against"; the letter (verses 11-16) is an accusation against the city. "One letter" is the Aramaic way of saying "a letter".

decisions.choice: the chief officer (Balanced, Readable); the commander (Literal)
decisions.reason: "Master of decree" is given an English official title; meaning decision m2 explains it. Readable calls Shimshai "the secretary" so the word is not confused with Ezra's title "scribe".

records.source: אֱדַ֜יִן רְח֣וּם בְּעֵל־טְעֵ֗ם וְשִׁמְשַׁי֙ סָֽפְרָ֔א וּשְׁאָ֖ר כְּנָוָתְה֑וֹן דִּ֠ינָיֵאוַאֲפַרְסַתְכָיֵ֞א טַרְפְּלָיֵ֣א אֲפָֽרְסָיֵ֗א אַרְכְּוָיֵ֤א בָבְלָיֵא֙ שֽׁוּשַׁנְכָיֵ֔א דֶּהָיֵ֖א עֵלְמָיֵֽא׃
records.gloss: Then Rehum, master of decree, and Shimshai the scribe and [the] rest of their associates, the Dinaites and the Apharsathchites, the Tarpelites, the Apharsites, the Erechites, the Babylonians, the Susanchites, the Dehavites, the Elamites,
pieces: Then Rehum the chief officer and Shimshai the scribe wrote, with the rest of their associates: the Dinaites, the Apharsathchites, the Tarpelites, the Apharsites, the people of Erech, Babylon and Susa, the Dehavites, the Elamites,

L.9: Then Rehum the commander and Shimshai the scribe and the rest of their associates, the Dinaites and the Apharsathchites, the Tarpelites, the Apharsites, the Erechites, the Babylonians, the Susanchites, the Dehavites, the Elamites,

R.9: Rehum the chief officer and Shimshai the secretary wrote it together with all their associates. These included the Dinaites, Apharsathchites, Tarpelites and Apharsites, the people from the cities of Erech, Babylon and Susa, and the Dehavites and Elamites.

decisions.choice: Then Rehum ...: the heading of the letter, naming its senders
decisions.reason: Verses 9-10 have no verb of their own. They list who sent the letter, in the manner of an official letter's heading, and carry on from "wrote" in verse 8. The list ends with "and now" at the end of verse 10.

decisions.choice: Dinaites, Apharsathchites, Tarpelites, Apharsites: uncertain names
alternatives: the judges, the envoys, the officials, the Persians
decisions.reason: These words are not known outside this book, and their meaning is uncertain. They may be peoples, like the names after them; but several may be Persian titles of officials: the first may mean judges, the second (compare 5:6; 6:6) a kind of envoy or official, and the fourth may mean Persians or a further rank of officials. They are kept as names here.

decisions.choice: Erech, Babylon, Susa and Elam: peoples brought from the east
decisions.reason: Erech (Uruk) and Babylon were old cities of Babylonia (Genesis 10:10). Susa was the capital of Elam, east of Babylonia, and later a royal city of Persia (Nehemiah 1:1; Esther 1:2). Peoples from these places had been settled in Samaria by the Assyrian kings (verse 10).

decisions.choice: the Dehavites: the reading of the Hebrew margin
alternatives: the people of Susa, that is, the Elamites
decisions.reason: The scribes' marginal reading gives a people's name, the Dehavites, otherwise unknown. The consonants of the written text can also be read as "that is", giving "the Susanchites, that is, the Elamites", which fits Susa being in Elam.

decisions.choice: wrote
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable repeat "wrote" from verse 8, which the heading leaves out; Literal keeps the bare list, ending with a comma as the sentence runs on.

decisions.choice: the people of Erech, Babylon and Susa
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name the cities instead of the forms "Erechites" and "Susanchites", which Literal keeps.

records.source: וּשְׁאָ֣ר אֻמַּיָּ֗א דִּ֤י הַגְלִי֙ אָסְנַפַּר֙ רַבָּ֣א וְיַקִּירָ֔א וְהוֹתֵ֣ב הִמּ֔וֹ בְּקִרְיָ֖ה דִּ֣י שָׁמְרָ֑יִן וּשְׁאָ֥ר עֲבַֽר־נַהֲרָ֖ה וּכְעֶֽנֶת׃
records.gloss: and [the] rest of the nations whom deported Osnappar the great and the noble and settled them in [the] cities of Samaria and [the] rest of Beyond the River, and now.
pieces: and the rest of the peoples whom the great and noble Osnappar deported and settled in the cities of Samaria and in the rest of the province Beyond the River, and so on.

L.10: and the rest of the nations whom the great and noble Osnappar deported and settled in the cities of Samaria and the rest of Beyond the River, and now.

R.10: They also included the other peoples whom the great and famous Osnappar had taken from their homelands and settled in the cities of Samaria and the rest of the province west of the Euphrates. And so on.

decisions.choice: Osnappar: probably Ashurbanipal, king of Assyria
decisions.reason: Osnappar is most likely Ashurbanipal, who ruled Assyria about 668 to 627 BC after Esarhaddon (verse 2). He fought against Babylon and Elam, and the peoples named in verse 9 may have been deported after those wars. The name is not found elsewhere in the Bible.

decisions.choice: Beyond the River: the Persian province west of the Euphrates
decisions.reason: "The River" is the Euphrates. Seen from the Persian capitals, the land beyond it was the province that held Syria, Phoenicia, Samaria and Judah. It is the official name of the province throughout Ezra and Nehemiah (Nehemiah 2:7).

decisions.choice: and now: and so forth
decisions.reason: The word marks a pause or move on in an Aramaic letter. Here, after the list of senders and before the narrator's "This is the copy" in verse 11, it most likely means "and so on": the narrator shortens the heading.

decisions.choice: the province Beyond the River (Balanced); the province west of the Euphrates (Readable)
decisions.reason: The Ezra term list gives these wordings; Literal keeps "Beyond the River".

decisions.choice: had taken from their homelands
decisions.reason: Readable says "deported" in plain words.

records.source: דְּנָה֙ פַּרְשֶׁ֣גֶן אִגַּרְתָּ֔א דִּ֚י שְׁלַ֣חוּ עֲל֔וֹהִי עַל־אַרְתַּחְשַׁ֖שְׂתְּא מַלְכָּ֑א עַבְדָ֛יךְאֱנָ֥שׁ עֲבַֽר־נַהֲרָ֖ה וּכְעֶֽנֶת׃פ
records.gloss: This [is the] copy of the letter which they sent to him, to Artaxerxes the king: your servants, [the] men of Beyond the River, and now.
pieces: This is a copy of the letter they sent to him: "To King Artaxerxes, from your servants, the men of the province Beyond the River. And now:

L.11: This is the copy of the letter that they sent to him, to Artaxerxes the king: "Your servants, the men of Beyond the River, and now.

R.11: Here is a copy of the letter they sent: "To King Artaxerxes, from your servants, the people of the province west of the Euphrates. Here is our message:

decisions.choice: the copy: the text of the letter, quoted
decisions.reason: The word is a Persian term for a copy or written text of a document (verse 23; 5:6). The writer quotes the letter from records, as he quotes the other documents in these chapters.

decisions.choice: your servants: the polite self-description of officials writing to a king
decisions.reason: Those who write call themselves the king's servants, as subjects and officials of the empire did in addressing him; here it means his officials (compare 5:11).

decisions.choice: and now: the formula that turns to the business of the letter
decisions.reason: In Aramaic letters this word ends the greeting and leads into the message itself (7:12).

decisions.choice: To King Artaxerxes, from your servants
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable set out the letter's address the way an English letter would; Literal keeps the order of the Aramaic. The quotation runs to the end of verse 16.

decisions.choice: the men (Balanced); the people (Readable)
decisions.reason: Readable says "people", since the senders stand for the whole province; Literal and Balanced keep "men", since the writers are named officials.

records.source: יְדִ֨יעַ֙ לֶהֱוֵ֣א לְמַלְכָּ֔א דִּ֣י יְהוּדָיֵ֗א דִּ֤י סְלִ֨קוּ֙ מִן־לְוָתָ֔ךְ עֲלֶ֥ינָא אֲת֖וֹ לִירוּשְׁלֶ֑ם קִרְיְתָ֨א מָֽרָדְתָּ֤א וּבִֽישְׁתָּא֙בָּנַ֔יִן וְשׁוּרַיָּ֣א שַׁכְלִ֔ילוּ וְאֻשַּׁיָּ֖א יַחִֽיטוּ׃
records.gloss: Known let it be to the king that the Jews who came up from beside you to us have come to Jerusalem; the city the rebellious and the evil they are building, and the walls they have finished, and the foundations they are joining.
pieces: Let the king know that the Jews who came up from you to us have gone to Jerusalem. They are rebuilding that rebellious and wicked city. They have finished the walls and are repairing the foundations.

L.12: Let it be known to the king that the Jews who came up from you to us have come to Jerusalem. They are building the rebellious and evil city; they have finished the walls and are repairing the foundations.

R.12: We want you, the king, to know that the Jews who came here from you have arrived in Jerusalem. They are rebuilding that wicked city that is always rebelling. They have finished the walls and are repairing the foundations.

decisions.choice: the Jews who came up from you: a group that came in Artaxerxes' reign
decisions.reason: The letter speaks of Jews who had come from the king's own lands to Jerusalem in his reign. This may be the group that came with Ezra (7:1-9) or another not recorded. "Jews" here is the name used by outsiders for the people of Judah (verse 23; 5:1).

decisions.choice: they have finished the walls: the accusers overstate
decisions.reason: The verb is in a completed form: "they have finished the walls". The Hebrew margin points it slightly differently, with the same sense. Putting the finished walls before the foundations sounds like an overstatement meant to alarm the king; in verses 13 and 16 they speak of the walls being finished in the future.

decisions.choice: repairing the foundations: joining or restoring them
decisions.reason: The verb is rare; it seems to mean "to join" or "to repair", here of restoring the foundations of the wall.

decisions.choice: that rebellious and wicked city
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say "that" for the Aramaic article, which here points to a city the king is supposed to know of. Readable turns "rebellious" into "always rebelling".

records.source: כְּעַ֗ן יְדִ֨יעַ֙ לֶהֱוֵ֣א לְמַלְכָּ֔א דִּ֠י הֵ֣ן קִרְיְתָ֥א דָךְ֙ תִּתְבְּנֵ֔א וְשׁוּרַיָּ֖ה יִֽשְׁתַּכְלְל֑וּן מִנְדָּֽה־בְל֤וֹ וַהֲלָךְ֙ לָ֣א יִנְתְּנ֔וּן וְאַפְּתֹ֥ם מַלְכִ֖ים תְּהַנְזִֽק׃
records.gloss: Now known let it be to the king that if the city this is built and the walls are finished, tribute, tax and toll they will not give, and at last [the revenue of the] kings it will damage.
pieces: Now let the king know that if this city is rebuilt and its walls are finished, they will not pay tribute, tax or duty, and in the end the royal revenue will suffer.

L.13: Now let it be known to the king that if this city is built and the walls are finished, they will not pay tribute, tax or toll, and in the end it will damage the [revenue of the] kings.

R.13: You should also know that if this city is rebuilt and its walls are finished, the people will stop paying taxes of every kind, and in the end the king will lose money.

decisions.choice: tribute, tax and toll: the kinds of royal tax
decisions.reason: The three words cover the taxes of the Persian empire: a payment in money, a tax on goods or produce, and a toll or land tax. Exactly which was which is not certain; together they mean every kind of tax due to the king (verse 20; 7:24).

decisions.choice: at last it will damage kings: the royal treasury will lose
alternatives: surely it will damage the kings
decisions.reason: The word for "at last" is a Persian loanword that may mean "in the end" or "surely". "Kings" here stands for the royal house and its income; the sentence is short, and the sense must be filled out.

decisions.choice: taxes of every kind
decisions.reason: Readable gives the sense of the three tax words together (meaning decision m1).

records.source: כְּעַ֗ן כָּל־קֳבֵל֙ דִּֽי־מְלַ֤ח הֵֽיכְלָא֙ מְלַ֔חְנָא וְעַרְוַ֣ת מַלְכָּ֔א לָ֥א אֲֽרִֽיךְ לַ֖נָא לְמֶֽחֱזֵ֑א עַ֨ל־דְּנָ֔ה שְׁלַ֖חְנָא וְהוֹדַ֥עְנָא לְמַלְכָּֽא׃
records.gloss: Now, because that [the] salt of the palace we eat, and [the] nakedness of the king not [is] fitting for us to see, for this we have sent and made known to the king,
pieces: Now because we are bound to the palace by salt, and it is not right for us to watch the king being dishonored, we have sent to inform the king,

L.14: Now, because we eat the salt of the palace, and it is not fitting for us to see the dishonor of the king, therefore we have sent and made known to the king,

R.14: Since we are loyal to the king and are paid by the palace, it is not right for us to see the king dishonored. That is why we are sending this message to inform you,

decisions.choice: we eat the salt of the palace: we are in the king's service and bound to him
decisions.reason: To eat someone's salt was to receive his provision and owe him loyalty; salt was a sign of a binding agreement (Numbers 18:19; 2 Chronicles 13:5). The writers present themselves as loyal servants of the crown.

decisions.choice: the nakedness of the king: the king's dishonor
decisions.reason: "Nakedness" here is shame or disgrace: a loss of the king's honor and power.

decisions.choice: ending with a comma
decisions.reason: The sentence runs on into verse 15 ("so that a search may be made"), so Literal and Balanced end the record with a comma.

decisions.choice: bound to the palace by salt (Balanced); loyal to the king and paid by the palace (Readable)
decisions.reason: Literal keeps "eat the salt of the palace"; Balanced keeps the picture and says what it implies, Readable gives the sense only.

records.source: דִּ֡י יְבַקַּר֩ בִּֽסְפַר־דָּכְרָ֨נַיָּ֜א דִּ֣י אֲבָהָתָ֗ךְ וּ֠תְהַשְׁכַּח בִּסְפַ֣ר דָּכְרָנַיָּא֮ וְתִנְדַּע֒ דִּי֩ קִרְיְתָ֨א דָ֜ךְ קִרְיָ֣א מָֽרָדָ֗א וּֽמְהַנְזְקַ֤ת מַלְכִין֙ וּמְדִנָ֔ן וְאֶשְׁתַּדּוּר֙ עָבְדִ֣ין בְּגַוַּ֔הּ מִן־יוֹמָ֖ת עָלְמָ֑א עַ֨ל־דְּנָ֔ה קִרְיְתָ֥א דָ֖ךְ הָֽחָרְבַֽת׃
records.gloss: that one may search in [the] book of the records of your fathers, and you will find in [the] book of the records and know that the city this [is] a city rebellious and damaging kings and provinces, and revolt they have been making in its midst from [the] days of old; on this [account] the city this was laid waste.
pieces: so that a search may be made in the record books of your predecessors. You will find in the records and learn that this city is a rebellious city, harmful to kings and provinces, a place of revolt from ancient times. That is why this city was destroyed.

L.15: so that search may be made in the book of the records of your fathers. And you will find in the book of the records and know that this city is a rebellious city, harmful to kings and provinces, and they have made revolt within it from days of old; for this reason this city was laid waste.

R.15: so that you can have the records of the kings before you searched. In them you will find that this city has always rebelled. It has caused trouble for kings and provinces, and its people have rebelled against their rulers since long ago. That is why this city was destroyed.

decisions.choice: your fathers: the kings before you
decisions.reason: "Fathers" means predecessors on the throne, not only the king's own ancestors. The Persian kings kept the records of the Babylonian kings before them (compare 5:17; 6:1-2).

decisions.choice: a rebellious city, laid waste: Jerusalem's history against Assyria and Babylon
decisions.reason: Kings of Judah rebelled against Assyria (2 Kings 18:7) and against Babylon (2 Kings 24:1, 20), and Babylon destroyed the city in 586 BC (2 Kings 25:8-10). The letter is hostile, but its history is true.

decisions.choice: your predecessors (Balanced); the kings before you (Readable)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable give the sense of "your fathers" (meaning decision m1); Literal keeps "fathers".

records.source: מְהוֹדְעִ֤ין אֲנַ֨חְנָה֙ לְמַלְכָּ֔א דִּ֠י הֵ֣ן קִרְיְתָ֥א דָךְ֙ תִּתְבְּנֵ֔א וְשׁוּרַיָּ֖ה יִֽשְׁתַּכְלְל֑וּן לָקֳבֵ֣ל דְּנָ֔ה חֲלָק֙ בַּעֲבַ֣ר נַהֲרָ֔א לָ֥א אִיתַ֖י לָֽךְ׃פ
records.gloss: Making known [are] we to the king that if the city this is built and the walls are finished, on account of this a portion in Beyond the River there will not be to you.
pieces: We are informing the king that if this city is rebuilt and its walls are finished, you will no longer have any possession in the province Beyond the River."

L.16: We are making known to the king that if this city is built and the walls are finished, because of this you will have no portion in Beyond the River."

R.16: We want you to know that if this city is rebuilt and its walls are finished, you will lose control of the whole province west of the Euphrates."

decisions.choice: no portion in Beyond the River: the king will lose the province
decisions.reason: "Portion" is a share or possession. The writers claim that one rebuilt city would cost the king his hold on the whole province, a great overstatement meant to alarm him.

decisions.choice: lose control of the whole province
decisions.reason: Readable gives the sense of the idiom (meaning decision m1).

records.source: פִּתְגָמָ֞א שְׁלַ֣ח מַלְכָּ֗א עַל־רְח֤וּם בְּעֵל־טְעֵם֙ וְשִׁמְשַׁ֣י סָֽפְרָ֔א וּשְׁאָר֙ כְּנָוָ֣תְה֔וֹן דִּ֥י יָתְבִ֖ין בְּשָֽׁמְרָ֑יִן וּשְׁאָ֧ר עֲבַֽר־נַהֲרָ֛ה שְׁלָ֖ם וּכְעֶֽת׃ס
records.gloss: The answer sent the king to Rehum, master of decree, and Shimshai the scribe and [the] rest of their associates who [were] dwelling in Samaria and [the] rest of Beyond the River: peace, and now.
pieces: The king sent this reply: "To Rehum the chief officer, Shimshai the scribe and the rest of their associates who live in Samaria and in the rest of the province Beyond the River: Greetings. And now:

L.17: The king sent an answer to Rehum the commander and Shimshai the scribe and the rest of their associates who live in Samaria and the rest of Beyond the River: "Peace. And now:

R.17: The king sent this answer: "To Rehum the chief officer, Shimshai the secretary and their associates who live in Samaria and the rest of the province west of the Euphrates: Greetings.

decisions.choice: the answer: the king's written reply
decisions.reason: The word, a Persian loanword, means a word, message or decision; here the reply the king sent back (compare 5:7, 11).

decisions.choice: peace, and now: the greeting of an Aramaic letter
decisions.reason: "Peace" is the usual greeting at the head of a letter, wishing the readers well (5:7; Daniel 3:31). "And now" turns to the business of the letter, as in verse 11.

decisions.choice: Greetings
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable use the English letter greeting for the Aramaic "peace"; Literal keeps "Peace". Readable leaves "and now" unspoken, since the letter goes straight on to its business.

decisions.choice: The king sent this reply: "To Rehum ...
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable set out the address as part of the king's letter, as at verse 11; the quotation runs to the end of verse 22.

records.heading: The reply of King Artaxerxes

records.source: נִשְׁתְּוָנָ֕א דִּ֥י שְׁלַחְתּ֖וּן עֲלֶ֑ינָא מְפָרַ֥שׁ קֱרִ֖י קָדָמָֽי׃
records.gloss: The letter which you sent to us, made clear, was read before me.
pieces: The letter you sent us has been read to me in translation.

L.18: The letter that you sent to us has been read clearly before me.

R.18: The letter you sent us has been translated and read to me.

decisions.choice: made clear: translated, or read out plainly
decisions.reason: The word means "made distinct" or "explained". At the Persian court it most likely means that the Aramaic letter was translated into the king's language as it was read to him (compare verse 7). It can also mean simply that it was read clearly, word by word (compare Nehemiah 8:8).

decisions.choice: to us ... before me: the royal court and the king
decisions.reason: The king speaks of the letter as sent "to us", the royal court, and of it as read "before me", to himself.

records.source: וּמִנִּי֮ שִׂ֣ים טְעֵם֒ וּבַקַּ֣רוּ וְהַשְׁכַּ֔חוּ דִּ֚י קִרְיְתָ֣א דָ֔ךְ מִן־יוֹמָת֙ עָֽלְמָ֔א עַל־מַלְכִ֖ין מִֽתְנַשְּׂאָ֑ה וּמְרַ֥ד וְאֶשְׁתַּדּ֖וּר מִתְעֲבֶד־בַּֽהּ׃
records.gloss: And from me was made a decree, and they searched and found that the city this from [the] days of old against kings [has been] rising up, and rebellion and revolt have been made in it.
pieces: I gave orders, and a search was made, and it was found that this city has risen up against kings from ancient times, and that rebellion and revolt have been carried on in it.

L.19: And a decree was made by me, and they searched and found that this city from days of old has risen up against kings, and rebellion and revolt have been made in it.

R.19: I ordered a search of the records, and it showed that this city has rebelled against kings since long ago. It has been a place of rebellion and revolt.

decisions.choice: a decree was made by me: I gave an order
decisions.reason: The Aramaic "to set a decree" is the regular phrase for a royal order (verse 21; 5:13; 6:1). The king confirms that the records say what the letter claimed (verse 15).

decisions.choice: risen up against kings: Jerusalem's past revolts
decisions.reason: As verse 15 says, Jerusalem's kings had rebelled against Assyria and Babylon (2 Kings 18:7; 24:1, 20).

decisions.choice: I gave orders (Balanced); I ordered (Readable)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable turn the passive "a decree was made by me" into an active verb; Literal keeps the passive.

records.source: וּמַלְכִ֣ין תַּקִּיפִ֗ין הֲווֹ֙ עַל־יְר֣וּשְׁלֶ֔ם וְשַׁ֨לִּיטִ֔ין בְּכֹ֖ל עֲבַ֣ר נַהֲרָ֑ה וּמִדָּ֥ה בְל֛וֹ וַהֲלָ֖ךְ מִתְיְהֵ֥ב לְהֽוֹן׃
records.gloss: And kings mighty were over Jerusalem and ruling over all Beyond the River, and tribute, tax and toll were being given to them.
pieces: Mighty kings have ruled over Jerusalem and governed the whole province Beyond the River, and tribute, tax and duty were paid to them.

L.20: And there were mighty kings over Jerusalem, ruling over all Beyond the River, and tribute, tax and toll were paid to them.

R.20: Powerful kings once ruled from Jerusalem and controlled the whole province west of the Euphrates. People paid them taxes of every kind.

decisions.choice: mighty kings over Jerusalem: David and Solomon
decisions.reason: The records show kings at Jerusalem who ruled the whole land west of the Euphrates and received tribute. This fits David and Solomon, of whom it is said that Solomon ruled over all Beyond the River and received tribute (1 Kings 5:1, 4 in the Hebrew numbering; 2 Samuel 8:6).

decisions.choice: ruled from Jerusalem
decisions.reason: Readable says "from" Jerusalem, since the kings ruled the province from there; "over Jerusalem" in Literal and Balanced means the same: they were kings in Jerusalem.

decisions.choice: taxes of every kind
decisions.reason: As in verse 13.

records.source: כְּעַן֙ שִׂ֣ימוּ טְּעֵ֔םלְבַטָּלָ֖א גֻּבְרַיָּ֣א אִלֵּ֑ךְ וְקִרְיְתָ֥א דָךְ֙ לָ֣א תִתְבְּנֵ֔א עַד־מִנִּ֖י טַעְמָ֥א יִתְּשָֽׂם׃
records.gloss: Now make a decree to stop the men these, and the city this not will be built until from me the decree is made.
pieces: Now give orders to stop these men, so that this city is not rebuilt until I give a further decree.

L.21: Now make a decree to stop these men, so that this city is not built until a decree is made by me.

R.21: So give orders to stop these men from working. This city must not be rebuilt unless I give another order.

decisions.choice: until a decree is made by me: the ban is not final
decisions.reason: The king forbids the building only until he himself gives a new order. Later the same king, Artaxerxes, sent Nehemiah to rebuild the walls (Nehemiah 2:1-8).

decisions.choice: a further decree (Balanced); another order (Readable)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable make clear that a new decree is meant, which the Aramaic implies (meaning decision m1).

records.source: וּזְהִירִ֥ין הֱו֛וֹ שָׁל֖וּ לְמֶעְבַּ֣ד עַל־דְּנָ֑ה לְמָה֙ יִשְׂגֵּ֣א חֲבָלָ֔א לְהַנְזָקַ֖ת מַלְכִֽין׃ס
records.gloss: And careful be [of] negligence to do concerning this; why should grow the damage to [the] injury of kings?
pieces: Be careful not to neglect this matter. Why let the harm grow and hurt the interests of the king?"

L.22: And be careful not to be negligent in doing this. Why should the damage grow to the injury of the kings?"

R.22: Do this without delay. Do not let this problem grow and harm the kingdom."

decisions.choice: be careful of negligence: do not fail to act
decisions.reason: The king warns his officials against any slackness in carrying out his order.

decisions.choice: the injury of kings: harm to the royal house and its income
decisions.reason: As in verse 13, "kings" stands for the crown and its interests.

decisions.choice: hurt the interests of the king (Balanced); harm the kingdom (Readable)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable give the sense of "the injury of kings" (meaning decision m2); Literal keeps the words. Readable turns the question into a command.

records.source: אֱדַ֗יִן מִן־דִּ֞י פַּרְשֶׁ֤גֶן נִשְׁתְּוָנָא֙ דִּ֚י אַרְתַּחְשַׁ֣שְׂתְּ מַלְכָּ֔א קֱרִ֧י קֳדָם־רְח֛וּם וְשִׁמְשַׁ֥י סָפְרָ֖א וּכְנָוָתְה֑וֹן אֲזַ֨לוּ בִבְהִיל֤וּ לִירֽוּשְׁלֶם֙ עַל־יְה֣וּדָיֵ֔א וּבַטִּ֥לוּ הִמּ֖וֹ בְּאֶדְרָ֥ע וְחָֽיִל׃ס
records.gloss: Then from when [the] copy of the letter of Artaxerxes the king was read before Rehum and Shimshai the scribe and their associates, they went in haste to Jerusalem to the Jews and stopped them by force and power.
pieces: As soon as the copy of King Artaxerxes' letter was read to Rehum, Shimshai the scribe and their associates, they hurried to Jerusalem to the Jews and made them stop by force of arms.

L.23: Then as soon as the copy of the letter of King Artaxerxes was read before Rehum and Shimshai the scribe and their associates, they went in haste to Jerusalem to the Jews and stopped them by force and power.

R.23: As soon as King Artaxerxes' letter was read to Rehum, Shimshai the secretary and their associates, they hurried to Jerusalem. There they used force to make the Jews stop building.

decisions.choice: by force and power: with armed force
decisions.reason: The first word is "arm", a picture of strength; with "power" (also "army") it means they used force, probably with soldiers. Nehemiah 1:3 may describe the result: the wall of Jerusalem broken down and its gates burned.

decisions.choice: by force of arms
decisions.reason: Balanced gives the sense of the paired words; Literal keeps both.

decisions.choice: stop building
decisions.reason: Readable says what they made the Jews stop, the rebuilding of the city (verse 21).

records.source: בֵּאדַ֗יִן בְּטֵלַת֙ עֲבִידַ֣ת בֵּית־אֱלָהָ֔א דִּ֖י בִּירוּשְׁלֶ֑ם וַהֲוָת֙ בָּֽטְלָ֔א עַ֚ד שְׁנַ֣ת תַּרְתֵּ֔ין לְמַלְכ֖וּת דָּרְיָ֥וֶשׁ מֶֽלֶךְ־פָּרָֽס׃פ
records.gloss: Then ceased [the] work of [the] house of God which [is] in Jerusalem, and it was ceasing until [the] year two of [the] reign of Darius king of Persia.
pieces: So the work on the house of God in Jerusalem came to a stop, and it remained stopped until the second year of the reign of Darius king of Persia.

L.24: Then the work on the house of God that is in Jerusalem ceased, and it was stopped until the second year of the reign of Darius king of Persia.

R.24: So work on God's temple in Jerusalem stopped. It did not start again until the second year that Darius was king of Persia.

decisions.choice: Then: back to the time of verse 5
alternatives: then, after the letter of verse 23
decisions.reason: This verse returns from the later letters of verses 6-23, which were about the city walls, to the temple, picking up where verse 5 left off. The temple work stopped under Cyrus and his successor and stayed stopped until Darius, as verse 5 said.

decisions.choice: the second year of Darius: 520 BC
decisions.reason: Darius I's second year was 520 BC, when the prophets Haggai and Zechariah urged the people to build again (5:1; Haggai 1:1; Zechariah 1:1). The temple was finished in his sixth year (6:15).

decisions.choice: God's temple
decisions.reason: Readable follows the Ezra term list for "the house of God".
